note: Plain-language definitions written for this app. Educational only; not financial or legal advice.

terms.definition: The Federal Reserve, the US central bank. It sets the key interest rate that influences borrowing costs across the economy and tries to keep prices stable and employment high.
The price of borrowing money, as a yearly percentage. When the Fed raises rates, loans and mortgages cost more and the economy tends to cool; when it cuts, borrowing gets cheaper.
The general rise in prices over time. 3% inflation means what cost $100 a year ago costs about $103 today. Measured mainly by the CPI.
Consumer Price Index: a monthly measure of the average price of a basket of everyday goods and services. Its change over a year is the headline inflation number.
Gross Domestic Product: the total value of everything a country produces in a period. Growing GDP usually means a growing economy; two quarters of shrinking GDP is a common shorthand for recession.
A period when the economy shrinks: less output, fewer jobs, lower spending. Officially declared after the fact by economists, not on a fixed rule.
A small slice of ownership in a company. Its price is whatever buyers and sellers last agreed on, which is why it moves constantly.
An index tracking about 500 of the largest US-listed companies. When people say 'the market was up', they usually mean this index.
An older index of 30 large US companies. Widely quoted, but the S&P 500 is a broader picture of the market.
A US stock exchange and its index, heavy in technology companies. 'The Nasdaq fell' usually refers to the Nasdaq Composite index.
A loan you make to a government or company in exchange for regular interest and your money back at a set date. US government bonds are called Treasuries.
The yearly return a bond pays relative to its price. Yields rise when bond prices fall. The 10-year Treasury yield influences mortgage rates.
Cash a company pays to its shareholders out of profits, usually every quarter. Not all companies pay one.
Exchange-Traded Fund: a basket of many stocks or bonds you can buy as one share. An S&P 500 ETF gives you a tiny piece of 500 companies at once.
A company's total value on the stock market: share price × number of shares. A $1 trillion market cap means all its shares together are worth $1 trillion.
Initial Public Offering: the first time a company sells shares to the public and gets listed on an exchange.
A company's profit. Public companies report earnings every quarter; the stock often jumps or drops depending on whether results beat or miss expectations.
Bull market: prices rising broadly and steadily. Bear market: a fall of 20% or more from a recent high.
How much and how fast prices swing. High volatility means big daily moves in either direction.
A tax on imported goods, paid by the importer and usually passed on to buyers as higher prices. Used to protect domestic industries or as a bargaining tool.
When a country imports more than it exports (deficit) or the reverse (surplus).
Deficit: the government spends more than it collects in a year. National debt: all past deficits added up. The debt ceiling is a legal cap Congress must raise to keep borrowing.
Congress's yearly plan for what the government spends. If the bills aren't passed in time, non-essential parts of government shut down.
A monthly government count of how many jobs were added and the share of people looking for work but not finding it (the unemployment rate).
The interest rate on a home loan. It tracks long-term bond yields more than the Fed's short-term rate.
A grade (AAA best) that agencies give to borrowers, including countries, for how likely they are to repay. A downgrade can raise borrowing costs.

terms.match: \b(central bank|ecb|european central bank|bank of england|bank of japan)\b
terms.definition: A country's or region's money authority. It sets interest rates and manages the currency. The ECB does this for the euro.
QE: a central bank buys bonds to push money into the economy. QT: it lets those bonds run off to pull money back out.
Government money or tax breaks given to make something cheaper or support an industry.
Penalties one country puts on another (or on companies and people), such as freezing assets or banning trade, to pressure them without using force.
A Senate tactic where a minority blocks a vote by extending debate. Ending it needs 60 of 100 votes, so most major laws need bipartisan support.
A directive from the President to federal agencies. It has the force of law within the executive branch but can be reversed by a later President or struck down by courts.
The highest US court, with nine justices appointed for life. Its rulings on what the Constitution and laws mean bind every other court.
Congressional elections held halfway through a President's four-year term. All House seats and a third of Senate seats are up for vote.
The system that actually elects the US President: each state gets electors roughly by population, and 270 of 538 wins.
A special budget procedure that lets the Senate pass tax and spending bills with a simple majority, dodging the filibuster.
Drawing voting district lines to favor one party.
Paid efforts to influence lawmakers on behalf of companies, unions, or causes. Legal and regulated, and very large in the US.
A union of 27 European countries with a shared market and, for most, a shared currency. The Commission in Brussels proposes laws and enforces rules.
A military alliance of 32 North American and European countries. Article 5: an attack on one is treated as an attack on all.
Laws that stop companies from becoming so dominant that they can crush competitors or overcharge customers.
Government spending or tax cuts meant to boost a weak economy.
A company letting workers go, usually to cut costs, not because of performance.
A company buying its own shares back from the market, which leaves fewer shares and usually lifts the price of the remaining ones.
